deep.reconstruction:
Context. This page belongs to Gauss's lattice-point bookkeeping for Gaussian-integer residue problems (the biquadratic-residue work). On the previous page, sums of pieces of the form ΔS(...), together with symbols R(k), J_k and triangle counts S(P,Q,R), are being added up. The next page states, and then refutes, an 'inductive theorem' about least residues of (a-bi)(x+yi) mod p=a^2+b^2.

Notation, inferred from the formulas and verified below. Write t=x+iy with x and y real. [t]=[x]+[y]i is the componentwise integer part. J z is the integer part of the imaginary part. J t(a-bi)=[Im(t(a-bi))]=[ay-bx]. J[t](a-bi)=Im([t](a-bi))=a[y]-b[x]. S(t,t+a+bi) is the number of lattice points m+ki 'under' the segment from t to t+a+bi: x<m<=x+a and 0<k<=y+b(m-x)/a.

1) Theorem (gcd(a,b)=1). Gauss first wrote aRt, then corrected R to J:
S(t,t+a+bi) = a[y] + (ab-a+b+1)/2 + [ay-bx] - (a[y]-b[x]) = [ay-bx] + b[x] + (ab-a+b+1)/2.
Proof sketch (mine). S = sum_{j=1}^{a} floor((c+bj)/a) with c = ay - b(x-[x]) = (ay-bx) + b[x]. Write bj = a q_j + r_j. Because gcd(a,b)=1, the r_j run over 0..a-1, and sum q_j = (b(a+1)-(a-1))/2. Hermite's identity gives sum_{k=0}^{a-1} floor((c+k)/a) = floor(c). Hence S = floor(c) + (ab-a+b+1)/2, and floor(c) = [ay-bx] + b[x]. This is exactly Gauss's expression; the a[y] terms cancel.

2) General case, gcd(a,b)=n. Gauss first tried a constant of the shape n(n-1)ab/2 + ... and struck it out. He also corrected the numerator from ab-a... to ab-a+b+n. Final result:
S = a[y] + (ab-a+b+n)/2 + n[(ay-bx)/n] - n([y]a/n - [x]b/n).
Derivation (mine). Put a=na', b=nb' and split j = a's + j0. This gives a'b'n(n-1)/2 + n([c/n] + (a'b'-a'+b'+1)/2) = n[(ay-bx)/n] + b[x] + (ab-a+b+n)/2, which agrees with Gauss.

3) 'Also alle 16 vereinigt'. This combines the 12 pieces and the 4 pieces from the previous page into one total. The total is a linear combination of R1..R12, J5..J8, R(5+i) and R(12+½ or i), plus a remaining triangle count -S(9, 9+1, 9+1+2i).

4) Parallelogram. The vertices are t, t', t'+a+bi, t+a+bi. Gauss first wrote b[x']-b[x]-a[y']+a[y] and apparently struck it through. The final count is [ay-bx] - [ay'-bx'] when gcd=1, or n[(ay-bx)/n] - n[(ay'-bx')/n] in general.
Justification (mine). The lattice points with ak-bm=c lie on lines parallel to a+bi, spaced |a+bi|/n apart along the line. Such lines exist only for c divisible by n. The parallelogram cuts each such line in exactly one period, so it contains n points on each. The number of admissible c is the number of multiples of n between ay'-bx' and ay-bx, with half-open conventions.
errors: In the gcd=n formula the leading term is still written 'aRt'. It should be 'aJt' (=a[y]), as in the corrected first formula; this is an uncorrected slip.
The first attempt at the gcd=n constant (struck out) was wrong. The corrected value (ab-a+b+n)/2 is right, and the a/a slip in the numerator was itself corrected.

The first-written extra terms in the parallelogram count, b[x']-b[x]-a[y']+a[y], do not belong in the count of a translation-invariant parallelogram. They appear to be struck through; the remaining formula is correct.

'Alle 16 vereinigt' does not match a naive sum of the previous page's 'alle 12' and 'Summe aller 4'. Several signs are flipped (e.g. R1..R4) and the R10 terms vanish. This suggests a changed sign convention or recomputation; it cannot be verified from this page alone.
Boundary conventions (half-open intervals, points on the segment) are left implicit, as is usual for Gauss here.

results.what: Closed form for the number of lattice points under a segment of rational slope b/a starting at an arbitrary real point: S = [ay-bx] + b[x] + (ab-a+b+1)/2 for gcd(a,b)=1, and n[(ay-bx)/n] + b[x] + (ab-a+b+n)/2 for gcd=n.
results.modern_name: Lattice-point count under a line / floor-sum identity sum_{j=1}^a floor((c+bj)/a) = floor(c)+((a-1)(b-1)+2b... )/2 (Hermite identity generalization; reciprocity of floor sums)
results.usually_credited_to: Floor-sum identities: Gauss (third proof of QR, 1808) and Eisenstein (1844) in the special case; Hermite (1884) for the identity; general inhomogeneous forms in 19th–20th c. (Dedekind, Rademacher)

results.what: Number of lattice points in a parallelogram with one side a+bi equals n·(number of multiples of n between ay'-bx' and ay-bx).
results.modern_name: Counting lattice points via the linear form ak-bm (unimodular/fundamental-domain argument)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard geometry-of-numbers fact (Gauss, Dirichlet, later Minkowski)

results.what: Assembling 16 pieces of a lattice-point decomposition in the Gaussian plane, toward a reciprocity-type count (biquadratic residues).
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein (1844) for the published lattice-point proofs; Gauss's unpublished biquadratic work is known from the Nachlass (Werke II, X)

deep.surprise_reason: The floor-sum and parallelogram counts are elementary, and Gauss's use of lattice-point counting for reciprocity (1808 onward) is well known. What is mildly notable is the explicit inhomogeneous formula, with arbitrary real starting point and general gcd n, used inside an unpublished Gaussian-integer lattice-point program. This anticipates Eisenstein-style geometric arguments and Hermite's identity.
